Abstract
This study focused on determining the optimal laser powder bed fusion process parameters for fabricating pure nickel (Ni) 
reinforced with 10 wt% titanium carbonitride (TiCN). Using a response surface methodology (RSM) approach, the process 
parameters of laser power and scanning speed were systematically optimized to achieve the best combination of high rela-
tive density and hardness. The optimal parameters of 195-W laser power and 400 mm/s scanning speed yielded a relative 
density of 99% and hardness of 335 ­HV0.5 which is an increase of 106% of the hardness of pure Ni. A porosity volume ratio 
of 0.23% and pore sphericity between 0.5 and 0.8 were calculated using computed tomography analysis. The fine pores were 
homogenously distributed. Microstructural analyses showed that while the majority of the TiCN particles remained unmelted, 
partial dissociation into the Ni matrix was observed without the formation of new phases. The TiCN particles facilitated 
nucleation leading to grain refinement and improved hardness. The refined microstructure consisted of both columnar and 
equiaxed grains elongated along the build direction, while in the perpendicular direction, it predominantly featured equi-
axed sub-grains with a few sub-dendrites. The enhanced properties achieved make the composite suitable for applications 
requiring improved mechanical performance of high Ni content alloys, where its inherent properties are currently limited.
Keywords  Laser powder bed fusion · Nickel · Titanium carbonitride · Metal matrix composite · Microstructure · Response 
surface methodology
1  Introduction
Pure nickel (Ni) is a versatile and widely used material 
known for its properties of excellent corrosion resistance, 
high electrical conductivity, and thermal stability [1, 2]. 
High Ni content alloys such as duranickel and permanickel 
have been employed in many applications including electri-
cal spring contacts and thermocouples [3–5]. Due to the 
relatively low hardness of pure Ni of 150 HV [6] and subse-
quent limited strength properties, the lifetime of high content 
Ni components is sometimes compromised. Enhancing their 
hardness and mechanical properties without compromising 
their desirable properties could significantly improve their 
industrial performance and lifetimes.
One approach to improving the mechanical performance 
of Ni is reinforcement with hard ceramic particles. Ceramics 
such as TiC, SiC, and TiCN are promising materials due 
to their desirable properties of high hardness, thermal and 
chemical stability, and excellent wear and corrosion resist-
ance [6–9]. Research on the addition of TiC to Ni manufac-
tured using spark plasma sintering showed higher hardness, 
compressive strength, and improved wear resistance proper-
ties [10]. The addition of TiCN to AlSi10Mg increased the 
composite’s high-temperature tensile strength without com-
promising toughness [11]. The addition of TiCN particles to 
reinforce Ni alloys has not been studied and is thus the focus 
material of the current study.
While high content Ni alloys are typically manufactured 
using conventional methods, the application of laser pow-
der bed fusion (LPBF) appears to be limited [1, 12]. Thus, 
in the current study, the feasibility of manufacturing high 
content Ni alloys reinforced with TiCN using LPBF was 
investigated, with the aim of determining the optimal pro-
cessing parameters to fabricate a dense material having high 
hardness. Studies on pure Ni fabricated using LPBF have 
shown high relative densities up to 99% [1, 12]. However, 
the addition of TiCN as a reinforcement may pose some

challenges. The mismatch in thermal conductivities, melt-
ing points, and laser absorptivity between Ni and TiCN are 
likely to influence melt pool dynamics, solidification rates, 
and overall process stability. Thus, tailored optimization of 
the LPBF parameters is critical to produce defect-free and 
high-performance Ni-TiCN composites.
LPBF is a complex process influenced by numerous fac-
tors including laser power, scanning speed, hatch spacing, 
and layer thickness [13, 14]. The interplay of these param-
eters has a significant impact on the quality of the final 
product. Failure to optimize these parameters can result in 
defects such as porosity, cracks, and incomplete melting 
[15], all of which compromise the mechanical performance 
of the fabricated parts. Traditionally, optimization of LPBF 
parameters relied on trial and error methods, single factor 
experiments, process mapping, or energy density models 
[16, 17]. While these methods provided initial insights, 
they are time-intensive, inefficient, and limited in captur-
ing parameter interactions. Recently, the adoption of design 
of experiments (DOE) and response surface methodology 
(RSM) approaches has transformed the optimization pro-
cess [18–20]. These approaches provide a systematic frame-
work for designing experiments, identifying relationships 
between process parameters, and predicting outcomes with 
high precision thereby saving time and resources. In the cur-
rent study, a response surface methodology approach was 
developed to systematically optimize the process param-
eters of the Ni-TiCN composite to achieve the optimal 
density-hardness combination. The relationships between 
process parameters, density, porosity, and hardness were 
investigated. Computed microtomography was used to criti-
cally study the porosity of the optimally produced materials 
which was complemented with a microstructural study to 
establish further relationships between the LPBF process 
parameters and microstructure.
2  Methods and materials
2.1  Feedstock powders
Gas atomized spherical pure nickel (Ni) powder (D50 
36.42 µm from Praxair Surface Technologies, USA) and 
irregularly shaped fine TiCN powder (D50 = 9.34 µm from 
Höganäs GmbH, Germany) were used as feedstock materi-
als. The powders were blended using a tubular mixer set at 
50 rpm for 2 h to produce the Ni-10wt%TiCN composite. 
The mixing parameters were determined through in-house 
investigations to achieve homogeneity while preventing par-
ticle deformation. The powder morphologies and particle 
size distributions were analyzed using scanning electron 
microscopy (SEM) and the laser diffraction method (Saturn 
DigiSizer 5200-Micromeritics), respectively as presented 
in Fig. 1. The elemental compositions of the powders as 
obtained from the suppliers are summarized in Table 1.

2.3  Microstructural characterization and hardness
The relative density of the samples was measured using 
Archimedes’ principle in accordance with ASTM B311-17 
[22] and the rule of mixtures [23]. The theoretical densi-
ties of pure Ni (8.90 g/cm3) [24] and TiCN (5.08 g/cm3) 
[25] were used for the calculation. To determine the relative 
density, the bulk density of the composite material 휌Ni−TiCN 
was obtained using the rule of mixtures of formula provided 
in Eq. (2), 휌Ni and 휌TiCN are the densities of Ni and TiCN, 
and wtNi and wtTiCN are their respective weight percentages.
Phase identification, x-ray computed tomography (CT) 
scanning, and microstructural analysis were performed on 
samples produced using the optimal process parameter set. 
Phases and microstructures were analyzed in samples cut 
parallel and perpendicular to the build direction as shown in 
Fig. 2c. CT scanning was conducted using a Nikon Metrol-
ogy machine operated at 210 kV and a beam current of 71 
µA. Reconstruction was carried out using CTPro3D software 
with a voxel size of 13 µm. The reconstructed volumes were 
visualized in VGStudioMAX 2024.2, and porosity analysis 
was completed using the VGDefX algorithm. X-ray diffrac-
tion (XRD) patterns were obtained using a Bruker D2 Phaser 
diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.5418 Å) at 30 
kV and 10 mA. The 2θ range for the scan was 30° to 100°, 
with a step size of 0.02° and phases were identified using the 
crystallography open database.
For hardness testing, samples were cut parallel to the 
build direction and polished using standard procedures, with 
colloidal silica (0.04 µm) as the final polishing step. Vickers 
micro-hardness testing was performed using an EmcoTest

3  Results and discussion
3.1  Determination of optimal process parameters
The results for the relative density and hardness responses 
measured for the nine fabricated cylindrical samples based

The ANOVA results, along with key statistical indicators

Both models were found to be significant, with p-values of

the highest relative density. The high relative density con-
tributed to fewer defects in the sample, promoting a more 
uniform distribution of indentation load during hardness

with samples containing more pores, which acted as stress 
concentrators under applied indentation loads. Notably, 
the hardness values ranged from 284 to 335 ­HV0.5 across 
all samples, thus surpassing the hardness of pure Ni of 150 
HV [6]. This improvement of up to 123% can be attributed 
to the reinforcing effect of the TiCN particles within the 
Ni matrix.
Porosity plays a critical role in determining the relative 
density and hardness of the samples. Figure 5 presents the 
nature and distribution of pores influenced by the combi-
nation of process parameters. Although no cracks were 
observed, irregularly shaped pores were particularly evident 
in samples produced at high scanning speeds of 450 and 500 
mm/s. This observation is consistent with the lower relative 
density and hardness results obtained for samples produced 
with these process parameters. Irregular pores in LPBF parts 
are commonly associated with lack of fusion defects [28], 
a phenomenon that may be aggravated by the use of the 
irregularly shaped TiCN powders. A more detailed analysis 
of porosity using CT scans in the subsequent section will 
further elucidate this behavior.

Figure 6 shows the combined plots of the first and second

the optimal results are from the first print with the process

optimal process parameters, the error of prediction for rela-

depicting high model accuracy of prediction and reliability.

3.3  Microstructure and phase identification
Figure 8 presents the XRD pattern for the Ni-10wt%TiCN 
composite. Given the relatively low percentage of TiCN (10 
wt%), only three TiCN peaks are evident as seen in Fig. 8a. 
No additional new peaks besides that of Ni and TiCN are 
detected, suggesting that no new phases were formed dur-
ing processing or if present, their quantities were below the 
XRD detection threshold. Closer examination of the magni-
fied primary Ni peaks associated with the (111) and (200) 
planes in Fig. 8b and c revealed distinct peak shifts. In the 
XZ plane, the peaks display a pronounced shift to lower 2θ 
values while the XY plane shows a slight shift to higher 
2θ values. The shift to lower 2θ in the XZ plane can be 
attributed to two main factors. Firstly, residual tensile stress 
resulting from the rapid directional solidification typical of 
the LPBF process [34] can induce lattice expansion along 
the build direction due to thermal contractions upon cooling. 
Secondly, the partial dissolution of TiCN releases its atoms 
into the Ni matrix contributing to increased lattice spacing, 
as these atoms are relatively larger than Ni atoms (Ni has a 
smaller atomic radius of 124 pm [35] compared to Ti of 147 
pm [36]). The TiCN dissolution will be further explained 
with the SEM and EDS analysis. In the XY plane, the 2θ val-
ues are closely aligned with those of the initial powder, with 
only a slight shift to higher angles. This observation implies 
that the residual stress in the transverse direction is minimal, 
indicating a more balanced stress state in this orientation.
Figure 9 presents the EDS mapping and SEM image 
showing TiCN precipitation of the fabricated composite. 
Within the Ni-rich matrix, traces of Ti, C, and N are detected 
suggesting partial decomposition of TiCN particles during 
fabrication. TiCN has a high melting point of 3225 °C [37] 
compared to the lower melting point of pure Ni at 1455 °C 
[38] making it challenging to fully melt TiCN particles. 
Given the fine TiCN powder (D10 2.05 µm) used and the 
high temperatures in the melt pool during LPBF which can 
reach up to 5000 K (equivalent to 4726 °C) near the direct 
laser spot area [39], it is expected that some of the TiCN 
particles experienced partial melting. In addition, the SEM 
image shows the presence of both unmelted TiCN and pre-
cipitated TiCN within the Ni matrix. The primary TiCN 
precipitates are diamond-shaped and larger, implying to have 
been formed first from the partially dissolved TiCN. At the 
elevated temperatures, the dissociated elements of Ti, C, and

C and N, it readily combines and recrystallizes into TiCN 
as the melt pool cools. Since this in situ TiCN was formed 
directly from the liquid phase, it allows the nuclei more time 
to grow before the melt pool solidifies resulting in larger

and N atoms leading to the formation of TiCN precipitates 
within previously solidified layers. As these precipitates 
form within the already solidified regions, atomic mobility 
is reduced resulting in finer precipitates compared to the 
primary ones.
The microstructure of the samples fabricated using opti-
mized process parameters, both along and perpendicular to 
the build direction is shown in Fig. 10. In Fig. 10a and b, 
the TiCN particles are seen to be randomly dispersed within 
the Ni matrix, exhibiting good metallurgical bonding at 
the interfaces. The favorable wetting behavior between Ni 
and TiCN is known to promote densification and improve 
mechanical properties [40]. Remarkably, the microstructure 
reveals the evolution of sub-grains within larger grains in 
both build directions, implying that the addition of TiCN 
transformed the pure Ni microstructure into smaller and 
refined grains that enhanced the hardness. For the micro-
structure along the build direction in Fig. 10c, the typical 
epitaxial grain growth of LPBF process [41] and columnar 
grain growth observed in pure Ni [24] transformed into sub-
grain within the larger grains. These sub-grains comprised 
of both columnar and cellular grains yet remain elongated 
in the build direction. The elongation aligns with the build 
direction due to the directional solidification [42] and layer-
by-layer deposition inherent to the LPBF process [43]. The 
growth of both columnar and cellular structures arises from 
the random dispersion of TiCN particles within the Ni

matrix, which generates fluctuating temperature gradients 
and solidification rates [44, 45]. Furthermore, the presence 
of TiCN particles altered the solidification behavior of pure 
Ni by providing additional nucleation sites and pinning grain 
boundaries [46] inhibiting the growth of coarse columnar 
grains. The melt pool boundaries are clearly visible in the 
microstructure, with grains growing inward toward the 
center of the melt pool. At the melt pool boundary, the finer 
sub-grains transition to coarser ones toward the center, likely 
due to the faster solidification rate at the boundaries com-
pared to the center of the melt pool [47, 48]. Figure 10d 
depicts the microstructure perpendicular to the build direc-
tion, showing predominantly cellular structures with some 
equiaxed dendrites, contrasting with the original fusion lines 
seen in the pure Ni microstructure along this plane [49]. The 
evolution of microstructures into planar, cellular, cellular-
dendritic, columnar dendritic, and equiaxed dendritic forms 
is influenced by the ratio of temperature gradient (G) to the 
solidification rate (R) [15]. In the observed microstructure, 
a lower G/R ratio along this plane appears to favor the for-
mation of equiaxed grains, similarly to what was observed 
by Chen et al. [50]. The absence of fusion lines along this 
plane may be influenced by its further location away from 
the solidification direction, which reduces surface tension 
and marangoni convection effects [51], thereby enabling a 
stable solidification process. The presence of TiCN particles 
also reduces the nucleation energy, which increases the like-
lihood of nucleation. These phenomena collectively result in 
a microstructure dominated by equiaxed grains, with occa-
sional dendritic features.
4  Conclusions
The LPBF technique was used to successfully fabricate a 
dense, hard TiCN-reinforced pure Ni composite using the 
RSM approach. The use of RSM helped to investigate and 
optimize the laser power and scanning speed that realized 
a high relative density and hardness. The following are the 
main conclusions from this study:
•	 The ANOVA analysis showed that both laser power and 
scanning speed significantly influenced the relative den-
sity and hardness of the Ni-10wt%TiCN composite, and 
that a quadratic relationship exists between the process 
parameters and responses.
•	 Process optimization conducted using the RSM achieved 
an optimal set of process parameters of 190 W laser 
power and 400 mm/s scanning speed. These parameters 
yielded a relative density of 99.1% and a hardness of 335 
­HV0.5.
•	 The addition of 10wt% TiCN significantly enhanced the 
hardness of pure Ni, increasing it by over double up to 
106%. The use of fine irregular TiCN powders effectively 
minimized the lack of fusion pores and reduced pore size 
as confirmed by CT analysis.

Abstract: This study focused on determining the optimal laser powder bed fusion process parameters for fabricating pure nickel (Ni) reinforced with 10 wt% titanium carbonitride (TiCN). Using a response surface methodology (RSM) approach, the process parameters of laser power and scanning speed were systematically optimized to achieve the best combination of high rela- tive density and hardness. The optimal parameters of 195-W laser power and 400 mm/s scanning speed yielded a relative density of 99% and hardness of 335 ­HV0.5 which is an increase of 106% of the hardness of pure Ni. A porosity volume ratio of 0.23% and pore sphericity between 0.5 and 0.8 were calculated using computed tomography analysis. The fine pores were homogenously distributed. Microstructural analyses showed that while the majority of the TiCN particles remained unmelted, partial dissociation into the Ni matrix was observed without the formation of new phases. The TiCN particles facilitated nucleation leading to grain refinement and improved hardness. The refined microstructure consisted of both columnar and equiaxed grains elongated along the build direction, while in the perpendicular direction, it predominantly featured equi- axed sub-grains with a few sub-dendrites. The enhanced properties achieved make the composite suitable for applications requiring improved mechanical performance of high Ni content alloys, where its inherent properties are currently limited.
